newsitem.title: USA: US Oil giant merger could pose distributor risk.
newsitem.headline: US Oil giant merger could pose distributor risk.

text.p: Gasoline marketers and industry observers warn the proposed merger of the U.S. downstream operations of Texaco and Shell Oil Co. could threaten the livelihood of some distributors.

The merger talks, which center on the downstream operations of Star Enterprise, Texaco's joint venture with Saudi Aramco and selected Shell assets, have not yet resulted in a detailed plan. But many industry observers say that such a combination could be the beginning of a trend that puts greater control of the retail industry into the hands of the big oil giants.
The potential consolidation and the impact on independents is seen as part of a broader international trend after years of squeezed refining and marketing margins for oil companies.

"In 1986 there were 60,000 gas stations in France and half were independent. Now there are 20,000; none are owned by independents and 50 percent are owned by the major oil companies," said an industry analyst who refused to be identified.
"The independent (U.S.) gasoline industry ought to look at this as an indication of what can happen to them," he added.

Similarly, the organization representing independent retailers in the United Kingdom warned earlier this year that a price war set off by Exxon Corp's subsidiary there could "devastate" the independent retail sector if it was allowed to continue.
The three-way combination in the U.S. could bring together Shell's more than 8,700 branded retail outlets with Texaco/Star's nearly 14,000, capturing a 15 percent share of the massive U.S. market.
"Such a combination is aimed at destroying rather than enhancing competition among refiners and gasoline retailers," said Edwin Rothschild, Citizen Action, a Washington D.C.-based watchdog group.
"If allowed, it would set a dangerous precedent," he said, adding less competition among suppliers usually results in higher prices.
Not all industry observers foresee a shutdown of gasoline stations under the proposed merger, but many point to the some 915 independent branded distributors that could be at risk.

Stations are not at risk, but if Shell has a distributor in the same town or city as does Texaco they may not want to have both," said Tom Osborne of the Virginia-based Society of Independent Gasoline Marketers of America (SIGMA).
Osborne stressed the 27,000-member group has not taken any stance on the merger and is to discuss the implications of the move in detail late next month.

"We are not suggesting that this one merger will put specific companies out of business, but it could be part of a trend if allowed to occur and could put a an entire trade out of business," said Osborne.

According to industry figures, there are about 10,000 U.S. distributor companies of private and major branded gasolines, holding 60 percent of the market. The remainder is supplied directly by 'Big Oil.'
These companies, Osborne said, "rely on having a wide variety of suppliers. So when you combine two companies it looks likely it will reduce by one the suppliers available to these people."
In recent years, SIGMA says it has sensed the number of these distributors has been declining as major oil companies buy more retail outlets they directly supply.
Bob Bassman, a lawyer who represents independent distributors, agrees that some could be at risk but stressed it is still too early to determine what shape the proposed merger will take.
"Whenever there are fewer sources of supply it impacts first on the people at the rack. They have fewer sources of supply and as a general rule that trickles down to the customer," he said.
